**No. Don't approve the $1,000/day plan.**

**Why it doesn't fit**
- **It overruns the budget.** October 19 to December 31 is 74 days. At $1,000/day that costs $74,000 against $45,000, so the money runs out around December 2. You would have nothing left for the December gift-buying window.
- **The 3.2 ROAS probably won't hold at 3x spend.** Returns usually fall as you scale. The 1-day-view window also counts some buyers who would have purchased anyway, so the true return is likely lower than reported.
- **Inventory is tight.** A 10-week reorder placed today arrives around December 28. Ad sales, organic sales and your 30% reorder customers all draw from the same 4,000 bottles.

**Plan to run instead (about $42,300, with roughly $2,700 in reserve)**
| Period | Daily spend | Total |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 19 – Nov 1 | ~$450, ramping up | $6,300 |
| Nov 2 – Nov 19 | $600 | $10,800 |
| Nov 20 – Dec 1 (Black Friday/Cyber Monday) | $1,000 | $12,000 |
| Dec 2 – Dec 15 (before shipping cutoffs) | $600 | $8,400 |
| Dec 16 – Dec 31 | $300 | $4,800 |

**Next steps**
1. Place a manufacturer reorder this week so you have stock in January.
2. Set your break-even ROAS: 1 ÷ your gross margin per order after shipping, discounts and payment fees. Because 30% of buyers reorder, you can accept somewhat lower first-order ROAS.
3. Track blended efficiency each week: total store revenue ÷ total ad spend. Don't rely only on Meta's reported figure.
4. Guardrail: if 7-day ROAS stays below break-even for 3 days, drop back one spend tier.
5. Keep at least 800 bottles in reserve for repeat customers. Throttle ads if stock falls toward that level.

**What would change this**
- Spend more if ROAS holds above about 2.5 at $600/day and your margins are strong.
- Spend less if there is little sign that customers buy because of the holiday season.
